note.saw: A blank canvas: this is the first time the scene is painted.
note.changing: Everything is laid in at once, back to front: a wet-on-wet sky with a few clouds, four layers of fan-brush pines from pale lavender-grey to near black, pulled-down reflections, white ripple lines, the rock ledge with its foam, and grassy banks with ochre tips.
note.why: Bob Ross builds from the back to the front, so the far trees stay soft and pale while the near ones are dark and sharp, and the white foam is kept as the brightest spot so the eye lands there first.
note.idea: A mountain river winds out of misty blue pines in the distance and widens toward you until it tumbles over a low ledge of round brown rocks into a white foaming spill, with dark evergreens closing in on both banks like curtains.

note.saw: The pines were stacked sticks with straw-like yellow streaks, the rocks were glossy brown balls over a hard white sausage of foam, the river was a narrow channel, and the horizon was a flat grey block with two stray blurry circles beside a cloud.
note.changing: Pine branches become tapered, drooping fan-brush dabs with short yellow-green flecks on the lit left side, the river widens and bends to fill about half the frame at the bottom, the rocks are flatter and lit along their tops over scrubbed horizontal foam, and the horizon turns into pale luminous mist.
note.why: A fan brush leaves tapered, overlapping dabs, not uniform sticks, and scrubbed foam keeps the falls the brightest spot; a lopsided forest feels relaxed and natural, like his compositions.

note.saw: The river ran almost straight down the middle with the rock ledge laid across it like a ruler-straight dam, so the whole picture was a symmetrical stage set; the foam was a white rectangle and the grass looked like yellow straws.
note.changing: The river now enters left of centre, swings right to a falls on the right third and bends back toward the bottom left; the ledge is staggered with water pouring through the gaps and soft spray rising, the near water darkens with tree reflections at both banks, and the corners get cool violet shadows with short ochre-tipped grass.
note.why: Bob Ross never paints a river straight at you: an S-bend leads the eye in from the misty distance to the falls and back out, and an off-centre falls makes the scene feel relaxed instead of staged.
note.visionary: Takes all four of the critic's first suggestions: a staggered ledge, a dark wet edge beside the bright fall, spray over the spill, and dark banks with a bright centre.

note.saw: SavesFish said every piece looked too rigid: the ledge was a row of brown loaves, the upper river stood up like a striped curtain, the ripples were ruler-straight bars, the spray was a neat oval halo, and the bottom corners were a noisy carpet of maroon blobs and yellow straws.
note.changing: The ledge is rebuilt as five rounded stones of different sizes with a warm lit facet and no outline, a falling curtain of white strokes and a churned foam mound overlap their feet, the spray rises in ragged wisps, and each pine gets a soft melted body under its brush dabs.
note.why: Bob Ross's paint melts and flows, and only a few crisp lines, like a ripple, a shoreline or the light on a rock, should stay sharp; soft bodies with sharp accents make a scene look wet and glossy rather than drawn.
note.visionary: Takes the critic's four suggestions: lit rock facets with water hiding their feet, flat upstream water, torn spray, and a mossy left bank.

note.saw: The five rocks still floated on a white plate with no drop, no wet face, no shadow or reflection; the upper river had almost vanished behind the middle pines; the right shoreline ran down as a ruler-straight line, and a flat grey band sat behind the right-hand pines.
note.changing: The falls become a real drop, with a calm glassy slide above the lip, a dark blue-grey wet face below it and broken reflections of the stones in the pool; the pines on the bend are cleared so a bright ribbon winds from the mist to the falls, both shorelines wander, and a warm pale yellow glow appears low behind the far pines.
note.why: A rock is anchored by its shadow and reflection, and the dark wet face is what makes a fall read as a drop and the foam glow; Bob Ross always leads the eye in along the water, and his shorelines are soft, never ruler-straight.
note.visionary: Takes all four of the critic's suggestions: shadow and reflection under the rocks, a wandering right shoreline, melting the grey band, and a warm note low in the sky.

note.saw: The forest and the S-bend were lovely, but the falls were tiny, a drop barely a finger wide with shiny brown eggs for stones; the upper river was an evenly pale ramp, a pale empty hole sat beside the falls, the sky's strokes read as straight rays, and the front pine highlights were scattered like confetti.
note.changing: The falls get a taller drop, bigger knife-painted rocks and a heaped foam mound with blue-grey pockets; a dark green bank fills the hole beside them, the sky is blended softer with the clouds melted out, the left bank becomes a few big calm bushes lit on top, and the pine highlights gather at the branch tips.
note.why: In a Bob Ross painting there is one place the eye lands first and everything else quietly leads to it; a bigger, brighter falls framed by dark rock makes the white sing.
note.idea: A second artist with fresh eyes sets out to make the falls the true star: twice as big, framed by dark wet rock and darker water, with calmer banks and a softer sky so nothing else competes.
note.visionary: Takes the critic's notes on wandering banks, water pouring between the stones, a broken wet face, and yellow only on bush tops.

note.saw: The fall hung in the river like a framed window box with pale smudges at its feet; the upper river was nearly as white as the falls and read as a second cascade, the pool had lost its reflections, and the stones were glossy brown buns all the same colour.
note.changing: Big dark stone shoulders close both ends of the fall with the outer pours bending round them, the upper river dims to a soft blue-grey with distance, the smudges become thin spray wisps, the pool gets a dark shadow line and the stones' reflections back, one stone turns grey, and the corners lose their violet.
note.why: A fall is held between rocks, still water repeats what is above it, and air dims the far water so the brightest white is kept for one place; Bob Ross always saves his brightest paint for the spot he wants you to look at.
note.visionary: Takes all four of the critic's offers: stone shoulders, reflections back in the pool, a dimmer upper river, and true spray in place of the smudge.

note.saw: The stones were still glossy brown buns, a pale grey box hung in the pool beside the foam, the near water was as busy as the falls right down to the bottom edge, and the clouds were one even white.
note.changing: The stones get flatter knife-cut tops with a lit top and dark side plus a little moss at the waterline, the grey box becomes a soft shadow tucked under the foam, the pool darkens and calms toward the viewer, and the clouds get a soft lavender-grey belly.
note.why: Rocks in a Bob Ross river are cut with a knife, not polished, and near water stays dark and calm so the light at the falls looks far off and bright.
note.visionary: Takes the critic's suggestions to darken and quiet the near pool, give the clouds a cool belly, and break up the hard right end of the foam.

visions.seen: I'm standing on the bank with the cold air coming off that spill, and the whole forest leans in to listen. The far pines have gone soft and pale like breath on glass, and that white foam pulls my eye right down the river to it.
suggestions: The rock ledge across the middle of the river sits in one even row, like a little dam laid with a ruler. Maybe stagger it: push one or two rocks a touch higher and let one sit lower and forward on the right, and let thin bright streaks of water pour through the gaps between them. Under the lip, just where the rocks meet the foam, lay a narrow dark blue-grey shadow band. Falling water only looks bright when there's a dark, wet edge right beside it.

The water in the bottom half is sprinkled with white dashes all the way across. Try saving the brightest, longest dashes for a band just below the foam and down the center, and let the water near both banks go darker and deeper, with the big pines' dark greens pulled straight down into it as reflections. Dark water at the edges makes the light in the middle sparkle the way it does at the easel.

Right above the foam, in front of the middle-distance pine trunks, a soft white mist could rise off the spill, just a feathered haze about a rock's height that fades upward. Spray hangs in the air over every fall. It ties the waterfall into the forest, so the pines don't stand behind it like cut-outs.

The shadows at the feet of the big front pines, bottom left and bottom right, read as near black and brown. Let a little cool blue-violet into them, and let the grass tips catch the light only on the side facing the bright sky in the center. Shadows outdoors carry the sky's color, and a cool shadow makes the warm ochre grass glow.
visions.keep: The back-to-front steps from pale lavender pines to near-black curtains, the lopsided frame (taller on the left, a lower cluster on the right), the soft wet-on-wet clouds, and the foam being the single brightest spot in the painting.

visions.seen: Those long slanting sunbeams pouring in from the upper left have me squinting like I just stepped out of the trees, and the river now curls in and out of the forest the way a real one wanders. But the rocks at the falls sit on the water like a row of brown loaves on a white plate, and my eye stops there instead of tumbling over.
suggestions: The rocks across the falls, right of center, are all the same dark rounded brown, each with a thin white line along its bottom like a cookie on a plate. Picture them knife-cut instead: a lighter warm grey-ochre facet on the upper left of each rock, where those sunbeams hit, sliding into dark umber on the lower right, and drop the white underline so the foam and falling water overlap the rocks' bottoms instead of outlining them. Rocks only look solid when one side catches the light and the other turns away, and water hides the foot of a rock, it never draws around it.

The upstream river, the narrow strip of water between the middle pines just above and left of the rocks, stands straight up like a little curtain. Let it lie down: short horizontal light strokes that get thinner and closer together as they go back, and the far end fading into the pale mist at the horizon. Water only goes vertical where it falls; everywhere else it is flat and mirrors the sky, and that flatness is what makes the drop at the rocks feel like a drop.

The soft white glow behind the rocks is a neat oval, like a halo. You took the spray idea, and it is lovely. Maybe let it break up and rise: ragged, thin wisps drifting up and slightly right, in front of the pine trunks, brightest just above the lip and gone by mid-tree height, with no clean outline. Real spray is torn by the air and drifts with it, so a ragged edge reads as mist instead of a light bulb.

The flat dark-green slope on the left bank, between the big left pines and the river, has a long straight diagonal edge. A few tapped bushes and a broken, irregular top line there, with a thin lighter green cut along the water's edge, would make it read as a mossy bank catching some of that sunbeam light instead of a cut-out shape.
visions.keep: The diagonal sunbeams from the upper left, the S-bend that brings the river in from the mist and back out to the bottom, the dark water at both banks with the bright ripple band down the middle, the cool violet in the corner grass, and the soft pale far pines stepping back into the haze.

visions.seen: The rocks finally catch the sun on their tops and lose those white underlines, and I can feel the warm light landing on stone. But the water drops off that ledge like a sheet of paper, and I'm waiting to hear it roar.
suggestions: Right under the rock ledge, at center right, the falling water is a flat white block with pale blue ovals sitting on it like stepping stones. Maybe let it pour: curved white strokes that bend over the lip and then drop straight down, with thin blue-grey gaps between them where the dark rock shows through, all crashing into a ragged, bubbly foam line at the bottom. Leave out the ovals, or break them into small scrubbed dabs. Falling water shows its speed in long streaks, and the dark gaps are what make the white ones shine.

The open water down the middle, from the foam to the bottom edge, is white and grey dashes over dark green. Pull some of that sky blue down into it: a soft, pale blue wash under the brightest dashes in the center, fading to the dark green reflections at both banks. Still water mirrors whatever is above it, and with a blue sky overhead the river should carry a touch of that blue, so it feels like it belongs to this day.

Those sunbeams slant in from the upper left but stop in the air, and the pines they would hit look just like the ones in shade. On the middle pines left of the falls, give the upper left edge of each branch tier a few warm yellow-green tapped highlights, and leave their right sides dark. Where a beam lands, the light should show up on whatever it touches, and that ties the sky to the forest.
visions.keep: The rocks' new light tops and dark undersides with the white outlines gone (thank you for taking that), the S-bend of the river, the pale lavender far pines in the mist, the slanting sunbeams, and the dark tall curtains of pine on both sides.

visions.seen: The river finally has the sky in it: that pale blue under the bright ripples makes the whole bottom half breathe, and the water now pours off the lip in streaks instead of a sheet. But those five stones still hover above the foam like a little bridge with nothing under it, and I keep wanting to reach in and set them down in the water.
suggestions: The row of rocks across the falls, right of center, floats on top of a white mound with no shadow below. Maybe set them in the water: under each rock, a soft dark blue-grey wet shadow that the foam laps over at the edges, and a short, broken dark reflection of the biggest stones pulled straight down into the pool just below the foam. A stone is anchored by the shadow it makes and the reflection it leaves, and that dark beside the white will also make the foam glow brighter.

The river's right edge, beside the dark right-hand pines, runs down as one straight vertical line from the falls to the bottom. Imagine a wandering shoreline instead: a thin, broken light cut where the bank meets the water, a few tapped bushes and grass leaning over it, and the right pines' dark greens pulled down into the water in soft vertical strokes that fade toward the center. A real bank bends in and out, and a ruler edge is the one thing that still makes this river look cut out of paper.

Behind the right-hand middle pines, at about the height of their tops, there is a flat grey band with a straight top edge. Let it melt: feather its top into the sky and the far lavender pines, and let it thin out as it goes right, the same as the soft mist on the left. Haze has no edges; it fades upward the way breath fades on glass.

The whole picture is cool blue and green, even where the sunbeams come in. A whisper of warm, pale yellow glow in the sky just above the far misty pines, near the center behind the falls, would say where the sun's light gathers. Bob Ross often slipped a touch of soft yellow into the sky low behind the trees, and that small warm note makes all the cool shadows feel like shadows on a sunny day.
visions.keep: The sky blue pulled down into the river with dark pine reflections at both banks (lovely that you took that), the streaked falling water under the lip, the warm yellow-green taps on the sunlit middle pines, the slanting sunbeams, the S-bend, and the near-black pine curtains framing it all.

visions.seen: Now the river comes all the way down out of the glowing mist to me, and that warm yellow breath low behind the far pines makes the whole forest feel like late morning (thank you for that). But the stones at the lip have lined up like five loaves on a shelf, each with little white icicles hanging off its front, and the water above them slides down a straight-sided ramp instead of lying flat in the woods.
suggestions: The bright upstream ribbon, from the mist down to the falls at center, has two long straight diagonal banks, so it reads as a sloping chute. Maybe let both edges wander: a few soft dark bushes and pine skirts nudging into the water on each side, the ribbon pinching narrow where it enters the mist and swelling again just above the lip, with its shine laid in short horizontal strokes. Flat water is only as wide as its banks let it be, and a bank that bends in and out tells the eye the water is lying down, so the drop at the rocks becomes the only place it falls.

The five rocks across the lip, right of center, now sit in one straight row at the same height, each with a white tag of water hanging off its front like a tooth. Picture the water pouring between them instead: one or two stones lifted higher and one sunk almost under, the white curtains falling through the gaps, and the fronts of the rocks left dark and wet where the falls hide behind them. Water goes around a stone, it doesn't drip off its nose, and the bright pours framed by dark rock are what make a fall sparkle.

Under the lip, the dark wet face is a flat grey band with a straight top and bottom edge, like a shelf. Let it break up: darker in the hollows behind each pour, lighter blue-grey where spray catches the light, and its bottom edge eaten away by ragged foam. A wet cliff face is never one even tone; the broken darks are what make the white water glow against them.

The mossy bank on the left, between the big pines and the river, is sprinkled evenly with bright yellow dots like polka dots. Maybe keep the yellow taps only along the tops of each bush, on the side facing the warm glow in the sky, and let the lower parts sink into dark green and violet shadow. Light lands on the tops of things, and fewer lights make each one feel like sun.
visions.keep: The warm yellow glow low behind the far pines, the bright river now winding all the way from the mist to the falls, the dark broken reflections of the rocks in the pool, the sky blue in the lower river with pine reflections at both banks, the slanting sunbeams, and the near-black pine curtains on both sides.

visions.seen: The stones have finally sat down in the water (no more little stems under them like in the last render), and the long dark reflections pulled down below them make the pool feel deep and cold. But the river around the falls sits in a smooth, rounded cut-out like a keyhole in green paper, and the drop itself is so short I'd step right over it.
suggestions: Around the falls, where the river widens at center, both banks bulge out in one smooth balloon curve with a faint dark rim, so the water looks pasted behind the forest. Maybe let the bank come in front of the water instead: a few soft dark bushes and pine skirts tapped right over the edge on the left and on the right shoulder, breaking the line in three or four places, with a thin light shoreline cut showing only between them. When the land overlaps the water, the eye believes the water is lying in the land.

The falling water under the rocks is only a sliver, about the height of a rock, so the whole fall reads as a riffle. Picture lifting the lip: the rocks and glassy slide raised a little, and the white pours dropping two or three times their current length into the foam, with the dark wet face showing between them. A taller pour gives the light more distance to catch as it falls, and that's where a waterfall gets its sparkle.

The four stones are all the same warm chestnut brown and glossy, like eggs, while everything around them is cool blue and green. Let a little of the sky land on them: a cool blue-grey sheen across the tops of the wet ones, a touch of moss green on the left one nearest the bank, and keep the warm brown only in the sunlit upper left. Wet stone mirrors the sky, and those cool tops will tie the rocks into the river instead of sitting on it.

At the bottom corners, the dark violet ground meets the river with a soft, smudgy edge. Bob Ross always finished his near banks with one bright, crisp knife line of light right where the land meets the water, and a little dark shadow cast out onto the water below it. A short, slightly wandering light cut along each near bank would set the foreground firmly in front and make the river feel like it flows past your feet.
visions.keep: The rocks now resting in the water with their long dark reflections in the pool, the river winding all the way from the misty glow, the warm yellow light low behind the far pines, the slanting sunbeams, the soft pale far pines, and the near-black pine curtains on both sides.

visions.seen: The falls finally has some height to it: the white pours drop a real distance now, and I can hear them hit the pool (thank you for lifting the lip). But the whole fall hangs in the middle of the river like a little window box, square sides and a flat bottom, and the cool pool below has forgotten the stones and the bright water above it.
suggestions: The falling water under the rocks, at center right, starts and stops at two straight vertical edges, so it reads as a framed panel. Maybe close each end with rock: a dark, wet stone shoulder stepping down on the left end and a bigger one on the right, each lit warm on its top left and sinking into blue-black where the spray wets it, with the outermost pours bending around them. A fall is held between rocks at both ends, and dark stone beside the outer pours gives them an edge to glow against.

In the pool just below the foam, the long dark reflections of the rocks from render #58 have gone, and the water there is the same streaky blue as the rest of the river. Let them come back, and add a soft, broken, pale reflection of the white pours pulled straight down under the foam, fading within a short way. A thin dark shadow line tucked right under the foam's front edge would lift the mound off the water. Still water repeats whatever is bright or dark right above it, and that echo is what makes the pool look deep and still.

The bright ribbon of upstream water, from the mist down to the lip, is nearly as white as the falls itself, so the eye runs up the hill instead of resting on the drop. Picture it dimming as it goes back: a soft blue-grey with the far pines' reflections in it near the mist, and only the last stretch just above the lip catching full white light. Light and contrast fade with distance in real air, and keeping the strongest white for the falls makes it the one place the eye lands.

Around the right shoulder of the falls there is a pale grey-green smudge with a rounded rim, like a thumbprint on the dark pines. Maybe turn it into true spray: a few soft, ragged white wisps rising from the foam and drifting up and right in front of the dark pine skirts, brightest low and gone by half the tree height. Mist that comes from the falling water explains why the air is pale there, so it reads as atmosphere instead of a smear.
visions.keep: The taller falls with its long streaked pours and the dark wet face between them, the warm yellow glow low behind the far pines, the soft bushes now nudging into the upper river, the sky blue in the lower river, the soft cotton clouds, and the near-black pine curtains framing both sides.

visions.seen: In #69 you gave the falls dark stone shoulders at both ends, and for a moment it was held between rocks the way a real fall is. Now in #71 they are gone again, and the right end of the white foam stops in a clean vertical cut against the dark pines, with a pale rim around it, like a paper cut-out pinned to the forest.
suggestions: At the right end of the falls, where the foam mound and the dark wet face stop in one straight up-and-down edge beside the right-hand pines, maybe bring back just one low, half-sunk stone from #69, or let a dark pine skirt and a soft bush tap down over that corner. Then let the foam thin into a few ragged white dabs that fade into the shadow instead of ending in a wall. Take out the pale rim around that bank too. Water never ends in a straight line, and white going softly into dark is what makes the foam look wet instead of cut out.

The light comes from the warm glow low behind the far pines at center, so the big near-black pines on both sides are lit from behind. Picture a thin rim of pale yellow-green along the inner edges of their branch tiers, the right edges of the left pines and the left edges of the right pines, facing the glow, while the faces toward us stay dark and lose most of the small yellow flecks scattered over them. Backlit trees only catch light on the edge that faces the sun. That rim pulls the curtains into the same light as the river and points the eye inward to the falls.

The pool from the foam down to the bottom edge has the same even pattern of white streaks all the way down. Imagine it brightest and most broken just below the foam, then quieter and darker toward the bottom edge, with only a few long thin knife lines near your feet carrying the deep blue and the dark pine tops. Bob Ross always kept the near water darker and calmer than the water by the falls. That darker foreground sets the pool in front of you and makes the light at the falls look far off and bright.

The cotton clouds, upper left and upper right, are one even white all over. A soft lavender-grey on their undersides, melted in wet-on-wet, with the brightest white kept on their tops, would give them weight. Clouds are lit from above, and a gentle cool belly makes them float in the same air as the misty far pines.
visions.keep: The tall streaked pours and the dark wet face between them, the warm yellow glow behind the far pines, the soft lavender far pines melting into the mist, the S-bend leading from the haze down to the falls, the soft melted bodies of the middle pines, and the dark violet corners with grass lit only near the water.

visions.seen: The pool finally goes quiet and dark toward my feet, and the clouds have that soft lavender belly now, so the sky has weight and the falls glows far off (thank you for both). But the warm light behind the far pines has risen into a hard-edged dome like a sunrise on a sign, and up close the stones are dark buns with little green smiles and a white collar of foam drawn around their feet again.
suggestions: The warm yellow glow behind the far misty pines, at center, now has a crisp curved top edge, a pale dome sitting on the treeline from left to right. Maybe melt that top edge away completely, wet-on-wet: the yellow strongest just above the tree tips behind the falls and fading up into the blue within a short way, with no line anywhere. Light in air has no edge; it thins as it rises, and a soft glow will make the sunbeams look like they come from it instead of from a lamp.

On the stones across the lip, a ring of short white strokes wraps each stone's bottom like a collar, and each stone carries a row of little green crescents across its middle. Picture the foam only in front of and between the stones, overlapping their lower edge in a few ragged dabs, never circling them, and the moss as one soft dark green patch tucked on each stone's shadowed lower side near the water. Water hides the foot of a stone and moss grows where it stays wet and shaded, so this sets them down in the river and keeps them from looking decorated.

Just right of the falls, a thin pale curved rim runs from the right shoulder stone up and over toward the upper river, like the edge of a tunnel mouth. Let that line go: soft dark Sap Green pine skirts and a tapped bush coming down over that corner, with only a faint mist wisp in front of them. A light outline around a shape always reads as a cut-out, and dark foliage butting straight against the white water will make the falls brighter.

Left of the foam, low in the pool, there is a soft round grey-green disc, like a puddle of fog sitting on the water. Maybe drop it, or flatten it into a thin, dark horizontal shadow right under the foam's front edge, and let the big left pines' dark reflection pull straight down into the pool there instead. A shadow on water is long and flat and follows the edge that casts it; a round blob reads as a stain.
visions.keep: The pool darkening toward the bottom edge with just a few long knife lines, the lavender-grey cloud bellies, the tall streaked pours with dark wet gaps between them, the stone shoulders closing both ends of the fall, the soft lavender far pines in the mist, the S-bend from the haze down to the falls, and the near-black pine curtains on both sides.
